extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Montaigne and Renaissance moral essays; general readers of philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Montaigne's Essays (selected chapters) presenting moral and practical reflections on death, desire, difficulty, and glory. The excerpt offers prescriptive and descriptive aphorisms illustrated with classical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: A short death is the sovereign good
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A short death,’ says Pliny, ‘is the sovereign good hap of human life.’ Caesar preferred ‘the least premeditated and the shortest’ death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that prolonging death gives time for remorse and suffering; examples and authorities cited include Caesar's reply and Pliny's maxim, implying that brief, unprotracted death is preferable to lingering, torturous ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: One must be thoroughly resolved to kill oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no great matter to resolve to kill oneself in health, but it is hard to put the resolution into practice unless one be thoroughly resolved; attempted but weak thrusts often fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives many historical examples (Heliogabalus’ theatrical preparations; Lucius Domitius, Demosthenes, C. Fimbria failing to finish themselves; Ostorius completing the act) to show that half-hearted attempts to die often end in failure or give opportunity for repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy and firmness in facing death are admirable
rubrics_metrics.description: Constancy and calm contemplation of death (as in Socrates’ thirty days) are signs of true courage and serenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates’ composed preparation for death and stories of philosophers who fasted to the end (Pomponius Atticus, Cleanthes) are offered as models of a firm, thoughtful approach to dying rather than panic or theatricality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty augments desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Our desires are increased by difficulty and opposition: what is rare, forbidden, or hard to obtain becomes more eagerly desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne supports this with examples from love (Lycurgus’ decree, Poppea’s mask, farthingales), literary quotations (Seneca, Ovid), and everyday observations (baths, pilgrimages), arguing that obstacles and danger heighten appetite and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility and satiety blunt pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ease and possession produce satiety; what we have is soon contemned, while what we lack is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an old horse losing fervour with mares in his pasture, marriages kept by liberty to divorce, and the contrast between want and abundance showing both afflict us—Montaigne notes that facility leads to disgust and dulled passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidden things whet the appetite
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions and restraints tend to intensify desire; to forbid a thing makes people more disposed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by classical citations (Ovid) and examples of social artifices (modesty, veils, concealment) deliberately employed to increase desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles and opposition can be beneficial to virtue or zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversity and opposition may revive zeal and rouse people from complacency; trouble can strengthen commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests divine Providence permits the Church to be afflicted to awaken pious souls; similarly, removing means of dissolving marriage made marriages looser, implying that constraints and oppositions have complex, sometimes salutary, effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence and display of protection can invite attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit defences or showy protection often provoke assault or give an enemy pretext; open, unfortified estates may be less likely to be attacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne describes his own house kept open with minimal guard: ‘defence allures attempt, and defiance provokes an enemy,’ arguing that obvious fortification can supply motive and justification for aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is a distinction between name (glory) and the thing itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The name (glory) is external to the thing and not part of its substance; glory is an added voice, not intrinsic worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses theological and philosophical language to stress that glory is external and accidental, and cites authorities to show why seeking glory for its own sake is suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt of glory is a Stoic ideal: avoid seeking reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Chrysippus, Diogenes and the Stoics advocated contempt for glory, arguing pleasure taken from others’ approbation is dangerous and corrupting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts the Stoic and Epicurean injunctions (e.g., ‘Conceal thy life’) and warns about flattery’s corrupting influence on princes and the ease with which praise can be used to manipulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory can be valuable for its practical benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Glory often brings real advantages—goodwill, protection from insult, influence—which may make it legitimately desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne concedes that external rewards attending glory (social advantages, safety) justify desiring reputation in some contexts, distinguishing desire of glory-for-ends from glory-for-its-own-sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is vain if motivated solely by glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue loses moral worth if its primary motive is reputation; being virtuous only when observed is inconsistent with genuine goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne invokes Carneades and Aristotle to argue for virtue’s intrinsic value and gives examples (secret acts, behavior in absence of witnesses) to show the insufficiency of reputation as a moral motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune governs reputation and glory is largely accidental
rubrics_metrics.description: Glory depends largely on chance and fortune; merit and renown are often disconnected, with many brave deeds unobserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne remarks that fortune often precedes or outstrips merit, and that countless brave acts occur unseen—Caesar’s fame attributed to circumstance—so one should not ground one’s worth on public renown.

rubrics_metrics.name: A mind evenly balanced between equal desires is incapacitated
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mind is exactly balanced between two equal desires, it cannot choose either and is effectively paralysed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne discusses Stoic attempts to explain choice among indifferent things, arguing that perfect equality is impossible in practice and that some slight difference always inclines decision; he uses metaphors (bottle and ham) and geometric analogies.
